title: Without Jensen Huang, Nvidia's organizational structure isn't 'built to last,' management expert says
summary: Nvidia's flat management structure could pose challenges for Huang's successor, according to experts.
body: Jensen Huang resigned Thursday as CEO of Nvidia , the chipmaking company he co-founded in 1993, following public revelations of his extramarital affairs. Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer, will serve as the company's interim CEO . Huang's visionary leadership style and his central role in driving the company's strategy, combined with the company's unusually flat management structure, will make him especially difficult to replace, experts say. Huang notably had more direct reports than the typical CEO, with a "direct staff" of approximately 60 employees, he said in a March 2026 interview with podcaster Lex Fridman. "The more direct reports a CEO has, the less layers are in the company. It allows us to keep information fluid," Huang told CNBC's Andrew Ross Sorkin in 2023. Having minimal hierarchy has worked for Nvidia so far "because [Huang] has been a strong leader with a strong vision," says Jo-Ellen Pozner, associate professor of management at Santa Clara University's Leavey School of Business. But that structure could make the company's leadership shake-up even more difficult to navigate, she says. At companies with flat management structures, the CEO often has even more influence than they would in a traditional hierarchy, according to Joseph Fuller, professor of management practice at Harvard Business School. Nvidia's structure was "designed to adapt well in a world of change, either caused by us or affecting us," Huang said in a March 2025 conversation with Arthur Mensch, cofounder and CEO of Mistral. Since he directly managed the company's top executives, Huang held "a tremendous amount of power" at Nvidia, Fuller says. "He's the orchestrator," he continues. "He's the coordinator. He's resolving the disputes. He's allocating the resources." Now, the company has lost its top decision-maker, Fuller says. Without Huang, "there is likely nobody who is able to coordinate among those various people with their different expertise and domains," Pozner says, which could lead to a slowdown in technical work. There are some advantages to Nvidia's flat structure, says Denise Rousseau, professor of organizational behavior and public policy at Carnegie Mellon University. Having fewer management layers can strengthen "local leaders" in each area of the company, she says, which can help stabilize Nvidia through its leadership transition. But "nobody else has the big picture view" that Huang did, Pozner says, which makes finding a permanent successor within the company especially difficult. Moreover, with dozens of direct reports, it's unlikely that Huang had the time to groom one of his subordinates to take over one day, she says. Pozner predicts that Nvidia's next leader will steer the company toward a more traditional management structure. "I understand that a lot of people, especially in Silicon Valley, are averse to rigid hierarchies and the kind of structure that we expect from a legacy organization," she says. "But it's functional for a reason." Ultimately, Nvidia's current system is "not an organizational structure that's built to last," Pozner says. title: Cisco beats on earnings, says AI infrastructure revenue will double this fiscal year
summary: Cisco is trying to become a bigger player in AI after missing out on the early years of the boom.
body: Cisco shares rose in extended trading on Thursday after the maker of networking gear reported better-than-expected fiscal first-quarter results. Here's how the company did compared to LSEG consensus estimates: Revenue increased 24% from $14.88 billion a year earlier, Cisco said in a statement. Net income rose to $4.6 billion, or $1.14 per share, from $2.9 billion, or 72 center per share, a year ago. Cisco is trying to gain a foothold in the artificial intelligence buildout after missing out on the early years of the generative AI boom. The company's stock price is up about 35% this year as of Thursday's close, trouncing the Nasdaq, which has gained 9% over that stretch. Cisco raised its expectation for AI infrastructure revenue from hyperscalers to $9 billion this fiscal year, more than double the figure in fiscal 2026. "Organizations are turning to Cisco for our trusted, market-defining technology and our expertise to help them scale, secure and optimize their environments for the agentic AI era," CEO Chuck Robbins said in the statement . For the fiscal second quarter, Cisco said it expects revenue of between $18 billion and $18.2 billion, topping the average analyst estimate of $17.88 billion, according to LSEG. The company is projecting adjusted earnings per share of $1.34 to $1.36, beating the $1.23 average estimate.

title: United Airlines won’t let AI agents book your flight. Expert says you shouldn't let a bot do that for you, anyway
summary: AI agents can save you time, but an expert says decisions involving your health, wealth and privacy still need human input.
body: United Airlines said Wednesday it would be restricting artificial intelligence bots from its digital platforms, warning that allowing third-party AI assistants to access account credentials could expose sensitive personal information, lead to unintended purchases or other unauthorized account activity. The move is similar to Amazon's recent blocking of Meta's Muse agent from making purchases on its site. Still, AI agents can complete a wide range of tasks on your behalf. Instead of just asking Muse what the weather will be tomorrow, you can tell it to suggest an outfit based on tomorrow's weather forecast and book you a rideshare if it's going to rain, for example. Or, rather than just creating an itinerary for your next vacation, you can connect a payment option and have your Dot — OpenAI's agent offering — book flights, hotels and excursions for you. You can even have an AI agent buy and sell stocks through investing platforms like Robinhood. Relying on an AI agent for any of these tasks may come with mixed results depending on which agent you use, what data you allow it to access and the complexity of the task you've asked it to carry out. Because broadly, agentic AI is still in its infancy, you may not want to let an agent make decisions "anytime [your] health, wealth, or privacy are involved," says Shomit Ghose, adjunct professor at the University of San Francisco School of Management, and lecturer at the University of California, Berkeley College of Engineering. "You can have agents do interesting things for you, like categorize your spending, or flag unusual charges, or model what-if scenarios," he says. "Those are good things, but bad things would be moving money, making trades, filing forms. All those things should stay manual at this point." Here's what you should consider before outsourcing your whole to-do list to an AI agent. Though AI agents' capabilities are improving, they still operate in a fairly literal sense, which can create problems, Ghose says. If you tell your agent to book you the cheapest flight, for example, it may book you a flight at 3 a.m. or one with three layovers, unless you give the agent specific guardrails. "The bot only knows your context," Ghose says. "It cannot infer, as we humans are able to do, because of instinct and culture and education." Further, bots can still get it wrong even with a seemingly clear and direct command. They "treat all data as being equal," Ghose adds. So if it finds information on the web that is either inaccurate or subjective, it could give you misleading guidance or fail to meet your standards for the given task. For example, if you tell your agent to book you a reservation at a good barbecue restaurant, it may get you a table at a place that claims to be "the best barbecue in the world" on its website. But the restaurant may be in an inconvenient location or have poor reviews elsewhere on the web. Your command may need to be more specific, like asking your agent to check reviews on Google Reviews or Yelp. Depending on what task you've assigned the bot, the outcome could be rather innocuous. But when individuals consider letting bots make purchases for them, make changes to their investment portfolios or and the like, the result could be more consequential. "In the end, you want to ask yourself: Does the human need to be in the loop?" Ghose says. If you're booking a vacation, for example, it's reasonable to ask an AI agent to help make a decision on your destination based on the weather, your budget and other factors. But actually booking the flights and hotels "should still come back to me," Ghose says. He wants to maintain final say over major financial decisions. Doing so may even save you money. title: Alice Huang tied to Nvidia’s biggest Chinese competitor
summary: The woman with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had a relationship also owned stakes in companies that provided computing power to Huawei, a key Nvidia competitor.
body: Alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang may have owned stakes in businesses in China that benefited Nvidia's biggest competitor in China, Huawei, at the same time that she was in business with Nvidia and also reportedly having a romantic affair with its ousted CEO Jensen Huang . The connection between Alice Huang and Huawei was first discovered by analysts at private intelligence firm Tesari. The firm exclusively shared its findings with CNBC. Tesari, which uses artificial intelligence to collect evidence and specializes in national security investigations around the world, provides intelligence research to private companies and the U.S. government. This previously unreported entanglement may raise questions about Alice Huang's intent and conduct in her relationship with the CEO and whether Jensen Huang knew his romantic partner was closely connected with his competition. Jensen Huang has acknowledged having an affair, though the precise timing of his relationship with Alice Huang is unknown. The mysterious saga of Alice Huang involves a tangle of interlocking corporations and transactions that show her connection to entities that ultimately provided computing power to Huawei in China. Huawei is known as a Chinese government "state champion" in the technology and telecommunications sectors, meaning it receives enormous financial support from the government in Beijing so it can lower prices and undercut global competitors. It is considered a key part of the Chinese government's push for global technical dominance and is closely linked to the Chinese Communist Party. Businesses connected to Alice Huang were linked with supplying Nvidia computing power to Huawei, according to documents reviewed by CNBC, around the same time she and Jensen Huang were first publicly seen together, in December 2023. In 2024, Nvidia said Huawei was a top competitor , specifically in artificial intelligence chips including graphics processing units, central processing units and networking chips. "This activity, which surfaced through our analysis of Alice's network, warrants a national security and [technology] counterproliferation investigation," said Brian Andersen, Tesari's vice president for national security applications and a former supervisory special agent with Homeland Security Investigations. If the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry Security and Homeland Security Investigations found evidence that anyone transferred "controlled equipment" to Huawei without authorization, potential charges might include export-control violations, conspiracy and smuggling, Andersen said. The connection between Alice Huang and Huawei is so convoluted that analysts at Tesari told CNBC that based on their previous investigative experience, they suspect it was designed to deliberately obscure the relationship. Nvidia and Huawei did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment. Jensen Huang did not respond to a voicemail left on a mobile phone. Alice Huang could not be reached. title: Jensen Huang is out and Nvidia stock is down—what market pros say about buying dips
summary: Nvidia stock fell 5% on Thursday following the departure of CEO Jensen Huang. Some see it as a signal to sell, others an opportunity to buy.
body: Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang has resigned as the firm's president and CEO, the company announced Thursday. Investors reacted negatively to the news. By 2:30 p.m., shares of the chipmaking giant were down more than 5%, and now sit 31% below their high on October 6. It's easy to see why Huang's departure, which comes amid revelations of his romantic ties to a woman believed by the U.S. intelligence community to be a Chinese spy , has investors feeling queasy. The company Huang co-founded 33 years ago — and whose chips have powered the artificial intelligence boom — has grown into the firm currently valued at about $4 trillion under his leadership. "The premise here is that there is no successor to a generational founder," says Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of the Founders 100 ETF, which invests in founder-led companies. "It's that they're one of one, and what they bring from a vision, execution and grit standpoint is not replaceable." While some investors are exiting Nvidia positions based on that premise — Monaghan's fund must, per its prospectus — others will see the slip in Nvidia's price as an opportunity to buy a great stock on proverbial sale , he says. Looking purely at the numbers, the opportunity to buy a stock with Nvidia's prodigious projected growth at its current depressed price "happens once a decade, maybe once in a career as an investor," he says. In investing parlance, the latter group of investors is " buying the dip " — investing in an asset after a decline in its value in anticipation of a bounceback. Whether it's a prudent strategy for you with Nvidia or any other stock requires some examination, investing experts say — not only of the stock in question, but your own portfolio strategy. When an investment you own or are interested in declines, your first move is to examine your reason for buying or holding it, says Tom Hainlin, national investment strategist at U.S. Bank Asset Management. Ask yourself if whatever caused the slide has changed your investment narrative, he says. "Has it changed why I bought the stock or why I'm investing in the market?" If you own a diversified portfolio and the broad U.S. stock market has declined, buying dips is a relatively straightforward decision, investing pros say. Because the stock market has historically trended upward, each downdraft has offered investors an opportunity to add an appreciating asset at a discount. "If you have a solid, long-term investment, it's always attractive to buy the dip because you always get a new high," Jeff Buchbinder, chief equity strategist with LPL Financial, told Make It in August. "In the history of the S&P 500, every dip has been attractive because you eventually made new highs." Individual stocks have no such track record, meaning that a major slide should prompt you to re-examine the thesis behind any given investment, Hainlin says. That analysis is twofold. On one hand, you should rethink the position any one stock occupies in your portfolio. If it's a large enough chunk that a pullback is keeping you up at night, it might be worth paring the position back to put things more in line with your tolerance for risk, he says. And whether you own the stock or are thinking about buying, a dip is a good time to evaluate your outlook for that investment. If you plan to hold a particular stock for the long term, for instance, you'll have to weigh whether the short-term bad news could have a lasting impact on the firm's profitability. title: In a policy switch, the Fed says its October 2027 meeting will not see a vote on interest rates
summary: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh announced the move at his October news conference, though he did not set a date.
body: The Federal Reserve won't vote on a potential interest-rate change at its October 2027 meeting, a departure that is part of a broader initiative from Chairman Kevin Warsh aimed at reducing the central bank's market footprint. According to an announcement Thursday, the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee will set aside its Oct. 26-27 session for "the discussion of broad monetary policy strategy issues." Warsh announced the move at his news conference after the FOMC met in October, though he did not specify which meeting would be affected. In 2027, there will be seven voting meetings, with the October session set up as extra time for policy deliberation without a formal vote or post-meeting statement. The new calendar shows that the final meeting of the year will now take place in November. It had previously been set for December. "Now, what's the reasoning behind this change? To me, it's quite straightforward," the chairman said in explaining his rationale. "Getting policy right involves assessing near-term developments at timely, regular, and information-rich intervals." "But it's equally important we reserve time and space, as an intellectually diverse group, for strategic deliberations—for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons, focusing, as I say, on the left side of the decimal point," he said. Warsh has been critical of the Fed's prior communications strategy, saying policymakers spent too much time providing guidance on policy moves that handcuffed them when it came time to make decisions. Under typical practice, the Fed meets eight times a year, following with a vote on interest rates and then a news conference from the chair. Since Warsh took over, the post-meeting statement has been shortened dramatically. Moreover, the press question-and-answer sessions have been cut to around half an hour from their customary 45 minutes or so. Warsh said in October that the meeting schedule is another step in his plan to streamline communication. He indicated last month that the number of nonvoting meetings would increase to two in 2028. "I believe the setting of the meeting schedule and agenda is more than some administrative detail," he said. "It's an institutional choice, affecting the nature and the quality of our deliberations and, ultimately, the wisdom of our decisions. It's yet another change to get the conduct of monetary policy on the right track." The FOMC next meets Dec. 8-9. Its first meeting in 2027 will happen Jan. 26-27. Correction: The Fed's October 2027 meeting will not see a vote on interest rates. The headline in an earlier version misstated the year.

title: Here's what Colette Kress and Harvey Jones wrote to Nvidia employees
summary: Interim CEO Colette Kress and board chair Harvey Jones emailed Nvidia employees, expressing gratitude for "resilience, professionalism and continued dedication
body: On the heels of founder Jensen Huang's resignation as CEO of Nvidia , new interim CEO Colette Kress and board chair Harvey Jones sent emails to employees Thursday expressing gratitude and optimism for the future. CNBC obtained copies of the emails from a source familiar with the matter, who said Jones sent the first email and Kress replied shortly after. Follow CNBC's live coverage of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation "The Board, Estaff and I recognize that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period and I want you to know how grateful we are for your resilience, professionalism and continued dedication," Kress wrote in her email. The term Estaff is commonly used to refer to executive staff, the group of direct reports to C-suite executives at a company. Nvidia will host a company meeting on November 18 at 9am PST, her email said. Board chair Jones took a similar tone in his email, and praised Kress as "a key architect of NVIDIA's growth and capital strategy." "The Board has full confidence in Colette to deliver on our commitments to shareholders, customers, partners, and to each of you," Jones wrote. I believe deeply in this company and in its future. More than anything, I believe in each of you, in our customers and partners and in the vital role we play every day in the global economy. The Board, Estaff and I recognize that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period and I want you to know how grateful we are for your resilience, professionalism and continued dedication. Thank you. This company has achieved so much because of the work that all of you bring to it every single day. You are our greatest strength. You will hear more from leadership in the coming days about our future together, and we will host a company meeting on November 18 at 9am PT. We play a vital role in building the technology that is powering the AI revolution, and we have important work ahead of us. So let's move forward together, with the same determination and commitment that have always defined this company. I am writing to share an important update. Jensen has resigned as CEO and Board Member, and the Board has asked our Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress to serve as interim CEO while it conducts a search for a permanent successor looking at both internal and external candidates. I will serve as the first-ever Chair of the Board. As CFO for over 13 years, Colette has been a key architect of NVIDIA's growth and capital strategy. She possesses a deep understanding of this business and the markets in which we operate. The Board has full confidence in Colette to deliver on our commitments to shareholders, customers, partners, and to each of you. Jensen's contributions to NVIDIA are profound. NVIDIA is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. We pioneered accelerated computing, defined the modern GPU, and built the platform that powered artificial intelligence. The Board takes seriously our duty as stewards of this great company. The strength of this company resides in our employees, leadership team, technical strength and partner ecosystem. I am confident that under Colette's leadership, with the full support of the Board, we will continue to grow our business, and lead the industry forward. Thank you for your focus, your professionalism, and your commitment to NVIDIA.

body: A PMI still well above 50 gives little reason to doubt New Zealand’s recovery, so the small fall should do little to change the outlook for the RBNZ or the New Zealand dollar. The focus on fuel prices among survey respondents links New Zealand’s factory sector to the oil shock. That keeps input costs and inflation pressure in view, even as demand holds up. Election uncertainty is a near-term drag on business confidence that could weigh on investment decisions until a coalition is formed. Markets will look to Monday’s services index for a fuller read on domestic momentum. New Zealand’s factory expansion lost a little pace in October but held a solid footing, as Christmas demand and infrastructure work offset rising fuel costs and post-election uncertainty. New Zealand’s manufacturing sector kept expanding in October, though more slowly than in September’s strong result. The seasonally adjusted BNZ-BusinessNZ Performance of Manufacturing Index (PMI) fell 1.4 points to 54.9 from 56.3, BusinessNZ said on Friday. A reading above 50 means the sector is expanding and below 50 that it is contracting. October was a 16th straight month above that line. The detail was mixed but still solid. Deliveries rose to 61.4, and finished stocks were 58.0, just below September. New orders slipped to 54.3 from 56.8 and production fell to 53.9 from 56.6, but both remain well inside expansion territory. Employment was again the weakest component at 51.9, almost unchanged from September. BusinessNZ’s director of advocacy, Catherine Beard, welcomed more than a year of unbroken expansion. She said the softening in new orders and production was worth watching. She also said the Christmas build-up and steady infrastructure work suggest manufacturers will finish the year on a solid footing, even as input costs and the cost of living weigh on many firms. Survey comments turned a little gloomier. The share of negative comments rose to 56.4% from 53% in September. Respondents cited fuel prices, the cost of living and uncertainty following the general election. BNZ said election uncertainty is likely to linger until final results are in and coalition talks are settled. The regional picture was uneven. Business South had the strongest reading at 65.0, ahead of Canterbury at 57.9 and the EMA’s northern region at 55.5. The Business Central region slipped into contraction at 49.1. BNZ said every manufacturing subindustry expanded in October. The bigger picture is still positive. BNZ said the result supports its forecast of moderate manufacturing growth through the fourth quarter and annual GDP growth of around 2% in 2026. Its senior economist said that although the PMI moves around from month to month, momentum in manufacturing is firmly positive. New Zealand’s reading also compares well internationally. It matches the US and is above the global manufacturing PMI of 52.6. The services index, due on Monday, will show whether the slower pace is limited to manufacturing. body: Katayama’s comments make intervention a more serious risk for anyone pushing dollar-yen above 160, especially as the US has now been confirmed as a willing partner. Expect choppy, headline-driven trading around that level, with dealers alert to any reports of rate checks. The underlying pressure on the yen remains, though, as rising Fed hike expectations keep rate differentials in the dollar’s favour. Oil matters too: higher crude prices raise Japan’s import bill and add to selling pressure on the yen, which is partly why Tokyo is bringing forward energy subsidies. With the yen back near 160, Katayama is reminding markets that Tokyo and Washington are working together on currencies, and that both have intervened before. Main article: Japanese Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama stepped up her warnings over the yen’s slide, saying she is seeing one-sided and rapid moves in currency markets and will stay in contact with the US Treasury to respond appropriately. Her comments come as the yen trades back near 160 per dollar, the level that drew joint US-Japan intervention in the summer. Katayama said the US and Japan set out a shared stance on foreign exchange at their summit, signalling that Tokyo sees Washington as aligned on the need to curb disorderly moves. She declined to comment on intervention records. That came shortly after the New York Fed disclosed that the US Treasury bought yen in July, its first yen-buying intervention since 1998, acting alongside Japan’s Ministry of Finance. The wording matters. Japanese officials typically use terms like “one-sided” and “rapid” when their concern is growing. Naming coordination with the US Treasury adds weight, because Washington has now shown it is willing to put its own money behind the yen. Japan’s vice finance minister for international affairs, Atsushi Mimura, gave a similar message on Thursday, warning that it was too early to forget the summer’s intervention. The yen’s renewed weakness reflects a familiar gap. A resilient US economy, stubborn inflation and rising expectations of a Federal Reserve rate hike in December are supporting the dollar. The Bank of Japan, which raised rates in June and September, is widely expected to hike again in December. Until that gap narrows, officials are relying on words, and the threat of action, to slow the yen’s fall. Katayama also said the government has decided to bring forward subsidies for household utility bills this winter, paid for from reserve funds. The move aims to protect households from high energy costs. Elevated oil prices have pushed those costs up, and the weak yen makes them worse, because Japan imports almost all of its energy. For markets, the comments make it riskier for traders to push dollar-yen through 160. With both Tokyo and Washington signalling they are ready to act, the risk of another round of intervention is likely to keep the pair volatile around that level in the weeks before the BOJ’s December meeting. He is also pressing banks to extend more credit to Nigerian-owned operators so they don’t have to chase foreign financing. His 650,000-bpd refinery outside Lagos carried 7.9 trillion naira, about $5.8 billion, in debt at the end of June, after reducing the balance by 798 billion naira in the first half. The refinery’s recent share offering drew 5.85 trillion naira in applications from nearly 3.8 million investors. title: Hudbay cuts cost outlook as Copper Mountain improves
summary: The operating gains come as Hudbay prepares to help finance its Copper World project in Arizona.
body: Hudbay Minerals (TSX, NYSE: HBM) reduced its annual cost forecast again as Copper Mountain generated positive quarterly free cash flow for the first time since the company acquired the British Columbia mine in 2023. Hudbay now expects annual copper cash costs, after credits for other metals, of negative 55¢ to negative 35¢ per lb., down from negative 45¢ to negative 25¢, according to a statement Thursday. The negative figure means by-product revenue more than covers the costs included in that measure. Adjusted third-quarter profit rose 11-fold to 34¢ per share, Hudbay also said, short of the 36¢ average of analyst forecasts. The operating gains come as Hudbay prepares to help finance its Copper World project in Arizona. Gold by-product credits support the lower annual cost forecast, although working capital absorbed cash in the quarter and left free cash flow below BMO Capital Markets’ expectations, analyst Matthew Murphy said. “Despite ongoing inflationary pressures across the mining sector, particularly from fuel and consumable costs, Hudbay stands out as the first company in our coverage to lower its 2026 cost guidance twice,” Jefferies mining analyst Fahad Tariq wrote in a note. “At a time when many producers continue to grapple with cost inflation, the revision highlights Hudbay’s ability to offset industry-wide pressures and further strengthens its position as a low-cost copper producer.” Third-quarter revenue more than doubled to a record $765.9 million, the company said. Copper production rose 25% from a year earlier to 30,152 tonnes and gold output increased 30% to 69,513 ounces. Hudbay also lowered its sustaining cash cost forecast to $1.40–$1.80 per lb. from $1.70–$2.10. Annual production guidance remains 110,000–138,000 tonnes of copper and 217,000–272,000 oz. of gold. Sustaining capital spending is expected to finish $35 million below Hudbay’s $435-million budget. That reflects lower capitalized stripping, capital deferrals and efficiencies. Gold output exceeded BMO’s 59,000-oz. forecast and the 62,000-oz. analyst consensus, helped by higher throughput, grades and recoveries in Manitoba. Copper Mountain’s mill processed 43,500 tonnes a day in September and remains on track for 50,000 tonnes a day by year-end. “Importantly, Copper Mountain generated positive free cash flow for the first time under Hudbay’s ownership,” TD Securities analyst Craig Hutchison wrote Thursday. “We see growing evidence that recent operational investments are beginning to pay off.” Hudbay acquired Copper Mountain in June 2023. The B.C. operation’s turnaround plan included more waste stripping to improve access to ore and work to lift mill performance. However, quarterly copper cash costs of $3.09 per lb. exceeded the company’s $1.50–$2.50 annual guidance range, with full-year costs expected near the upper end. Hudbay reported $201.9 million in quarterly free cash flow, calculated as $313.9 million in operating cash flow before working-capital changes less $112 million in adjusted sustaining capital. The company’s measure excludes growth capital spending. BMO calculated a roughly $2-million deficit, using $215 million in operating cash flow after a $99-million working-capital build and deducting $217 million in capital spending. That fell short of the banks $58-million forecast and the $88-million analyst consensus. The different definitions explain why the company’s positive figure and BMO’s cash-flow miss coexist. Hudbay and Mitsubishi approved construction of Copper World on Oct. 21. The project, about 50 km southeast of Tucson, has initial growth capital of $2.1 billion. Hudbay is targeting first production in the second half of 2029. Hudbay expects its own capital contribution to the project to total about $500 million, starting in 2028. Mitsubishi’s investment, a precious-metals stream and planned project debt would cover much of the remaining requirement, the partners said when approving construction. title: Tighter regulation not enough to stop importing illicit gold to UAE: report
summary: Even with new regulation implemented in 2023, the UAE has not been able to better trace its gold imports, a new report shows.
body: The United Arab Emirates (UAE) is known to bridge the gap between gold-producing and gold-consuming countries, but a weak regulatory system has led the country to import at least 591 tonnes of illicit gold in 2024, a new SWISSAID report shows. The report used data from 2021 to 2025 and interviewed over 150 stakeholders to get to these findings and recommendations, and better understand the UAE’s role in the global gold market. Despite tighter regulations introduced in 2023 to promote a greater due diligence regarding imports and exports, massive quantities of illicit gold continue to be imported into the country, the report found. Illicit gold includes the metal that was either smuggled to the UAE without traceability or produced in countries with ongoing conflicts, including Russia, Yemen and Sudan. SWISSAID said the findings are important to the Swiss industry, as it is the main importer of gold from the UAE. “The findings of this study are deeply concerning,’ Head of SWISSAID’s raw materials unit, Marc Ummel said. “They show that the United Arab Emirates remains a hub for smuggled and conflict gold.” The 591 tonnes of illicit gold imported by the UAE in 2024 would be worth $74 billion at current prices. It included 453 tonnes coming from African producing countries, and about 137 tonnes coming from countries subject to international sanctions. This represents 42% of total gold imports into the UAE in 2024. The UAE became a top destination for gold production due to its business-friendly regulation and weaker due diligence requirements and penalties for non-compliance, but that also opened up the door to issues regarding illicit producers. Still, the country has made strides to create tighter due diligence requirements for gold sourcing with new regulation being introduced in 2023. The goal was to increase gold traceability and control, but that is still not the reality. Out of the 52 Emirati refineries that were reviewed for their 2023 to 2025 production, only two were fully adopting the new regulations, the report showed. Refineries still have a weak traceability system, receive gold from intermediaries, fail to conduct due diligence and site visits and seem to be regressing on regulation rather than enforcing the new one. The new regulations have increased transparency on how due diligence is performed in Emirati refineries, but it still isn’t enough to improve poor due diligence, especially when it comes to illicit gold, according to the report. In light of the results of their study, SWISSAID is asking the UAE to better apply its regulations so due diligence can actually be performed by refineries and gold traceability can increase for importers. It recommended that the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) put the UAE back on its list of jurisdictions with strategic deficiencies in combating money laundering and the financing of terrorism. It also asked that penalties for non-compliance should be increased or made public, for Emirati companies to share the names of their suppliers of mined gold and for the Emirati customs authorities to increase their controls. While the UAE is the top destination for gold linked to armed conflicts globally, SWISSAID said those conflicted affected areas shouldn’t be completely shut out from imports, as it would hurt the industry and legitimate miners in the region. The non-profit said that with proper due diligence on UAE’s part, those areas can still be a great source and help combat illicit gold. Switzerland is the top importer of gold from the UAE, having imported 420 tonnes of gold in 2024, and has already imported over 400 tonnes of gold from the country in 2026. Billionaire Robert Friedland announced the agreement Thursday on the sidelines of the Pakistan Minerals Investment Forum . Friedland is the founder and chairman of I-Pulse Inc., a US company that holds a majority stake in Ivanhoe Atlantic. He said Ivanhoe was beginning to establish a local office and expected to sign another agreement Friday. Mari Minerals, the mining subsidiary of Mari Energies, has several copper and gold exploration projects in Pakistan. “We’re forming equal partnerships,” Friedland told reporters when asked about the MoU’s structure and timeline. He said the company is seeking to bring international expertise to Pakistan to accelerate mineral discoveries. While Friedland indicated that Ivanhoe intends to pursue equal partnerships in Pakistan, he did not confirm whether the agreement with Mari Energies would follow a 50-50 ownership structure. The companies have not disclosed financial terms, specific exploration commitments or a timetable for a definitive agreement. The move gives Ivanhoe Atlantic a foothold in a largely underexplored mineral jurisdiction as Pakistan seeks foreign capital and technical expertise to develop its copper and gold resources. Security concerns and infrastructure challenges remain significant obstacles to attracting international investment. Friedland said Ivanhoe intends to draw on its experience in Mongolia, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Saudi Arabia as it establishes a presence in Pakistan. The Canadian mining entrepreneur told MINING.COM that Pakistan’s copper and gold potential is supported by a vast mineralized geological belt extending from Turkey and Iran through Afghanistan and Pakistan into western China and Mongolia. “Pakistan is profoundly unexplored,” Friedland said in an exclusive interview Thursday, pointing to advances in geophysical surveying, remote sensing and artificial intelligence that could help identify deposits more quickly than traditional exploration methods. He said the country sits along a vast mineralized geological belt extending from Turkey and Iran through Afghanistan and Pakistan into western China and Mongolia. The region hosts major copper and gold systems, but much of its exploration potential remains untested. Friedland also stressed that successful mining development depends on local communities sharing directly in the economic benefits, including employment, education and infrastructure improvements. Drawing on Ivanhoe’s experience in Africa, he said community participation is essential to securing long-term support for mining operations and avoiding disputes that can disrupt projects. Pakistan has been courting foreign mining companies to help unlock its mineral wealth, including plans announced last year to offer concessions to US investors as part of broader tariff negotiations with Washington. The country hosts major copper and gold deposits, including Reko Diq in Balochistan, one of the world’s largest undeveloped copper-gold projects. However, the investment push faces significant obstacles. Earlier this year, Barrick Mining (TSX: ABX) (NYSE: B) extended its review of Reko Diq amid escalating security concerns in Pakistan and the Middle East, underscoring the risks facing foreign companies operating in the region. Developing new mines will also require substantial investment in transport infrastructure, energy and skilled labour. title: A shortage of ore is causing a pricing revolution in copper - Mining.com
body: The decades-old system that the copper industry uses to price mined ores is fracturing in the face of an acute shortage. Since at least the 1980s, a once-a-year negotiation between a leading mining company and a large copper smelter has set an annual ‘benchmark’ price that is used across the market to determine how the two giant industries share out the profits of producing copper. But, with annual contractual negotiations coming to a head, the number of deals linked to the benchmark price has already fallen sharply, and is set to drop further next year, according to consultancy CRU Group. The shift is a major upheaval, affecting the pricing of more than $200 billion a year in copper ore, known as concentrates. A similar shift away from benchmark pricing that took place in the iron ore market nearly two decades ago was credited with delivering a profit windfall to miners. Under annual supply deals, miners typically deduct fixed treatment and refining charges from the price of concentrates to cover the cost of smelting them into finished copper. For decades, the first deal reached between a major buyer and seller has served as a benchmark followed by the rest of the industry. Over the past few years, constraints on mine supply — combined with a surge in smelting capacity and fierce bidding by traders — have driven benchmark charges to record lows. But they’ve fallen even further in the spot market, where TC/RCs are now trading at deeply negative levels, in effect meaning that they’re being added to the cost of concentrates rather than deducted from them. As supply negotiations kicked off in London last month, mining executives demanded that any fixed-price deals would need to be set at levels close to the spot market, according to people involved in the talks, who asked not to be identified because the discussions are private. Meanwhile, smelters warned that they were already facing such deep losses that they’d started cutting output and planned further reductions next year. Miners and smelters are set to meet again for crunch talks during a major industry gathering in Shanghai next week, but the debate over next year’s supply has become so polarized that many in the industry are questioning whether they’ll be able to agree a benchmark deal at all. In a rare move, Wood Mackenzie — which much of the market relies on for supply and pricing forecasts — has decided not offer a prediction for next year’s benchmark. “The challenge this year is that negotiations are taking place against one of the widest divergences between benchmark and spot conditions seen in recent years,” said Anna Xu, a senior analyst at Wood Mackenzie. The upheaval in the copper concentrates market comes after a surge in smelting capacity in China, which now processes more than half the world’s mined copper. For years, being the dominant buyer gave China clout in annual supply negotiations, but scarce supplies of copper ores have placed its smelters in a disadvantaged position. While Chinese smelters are still negotiating over a benchmark deal for next year, much of the industry has already shifted towards deals linked to indexes for spot TC/RCs provided by third-party agencies like Fastmarkets Ltd. and SMM. The trend mimics a shift that transformed the iron ore market in the 2010s, when top miner BHP Group pushed China’s steel mills into deals that gave them a passive exposure to price indexes based on the spot market. The transition, which came as iron ore prices surged on the back of the Chinese infrastructure boom, helped to deliver huge profits to the largest iron ore miners. And as the market has cooled over recent years, China has worked aggressively to rebuild its pricing power. The revised forecast presents another challenge for Wall Street, particularly technology stocks, homebuilders and other businesses sensitive to higher interest rates. Goldman now expects a 25-basis-point increase in December, followed by another quarter-point hike in March, potentially bringing the federal funds target range to 4.25%4.50%. However, the bank acknowledges that the second increase could arrive as early as January. The change follows October's hotter-than-expected consumer inflation report, which marked the third consecutive monthly upside surprise. Headline consumer prices increased 0.4% in October, exceeding expectations for 0.3%, while core inflation rose 0.3%, above forecasts of 0.2%. Goldman chief U.S. economist David Mericle believes persistent inflation will encourage policymakers to signal additional tightening at December's meeting. The bank expects inflation to moderate through year-end before renewed price pressures emerge in early 2027. Higher oil prices, tariffs, resilient consumer demand and substantial AI infrastructure investment have contributed to inflationary pressures. Goldman's outlook is less aggressive than Deutsche Bank's, which anticipates three additional quarter-point hikes through March, potentially lifting rates to 4.50%4.75%. Importantly, Goldman has also delayed its expected first rate cut from September to December 2027, with further reductions projected during 2028. The Fed's December 89 meeting represents the next major catalyst, particularly its updated economic projections and interest-rate forecasts. Investors should monitor core inflation, wage growth, Treasury yields and whether policymakers signal additional tightening. Persistent inflation could pressure richly valued technology stocks by keeping discount rates elevated, while higher mortgage rates could weaken housing demand. Bond investors also face risks if Treasury yields rise further. Conversely, softer inflation and moderating energy prices could reduce the need for additional hikes. For now, Goldman's revised forecast suggests investors may need to prepare for restrictive monetary policy lasting considerably longer than previously expected.

body: Jensen Huang's resignation as CEO of Nvidia whiplashed markets on Thursday, hitting the AI giant but lifting some of its rivals as investors tried to game out the ripple effects from the shakeup. Jensen, co-founder of the world's leading designer of the chips that power AI models, stepped down in the face of a board revolt following revelations he had two extra-marital affairs, including with a woman accused of spying for China. Chief financial officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO while keeping her finance role, and the board will consider internal and external candidates for a permanent replacement. Shares in Nvidia plunged 13 percent at the start of trading in New York before moderating. The stock, a component in both the Dow and Nasdaq indices, finished down 4.3 percent. The tech-focused Nasdaq had a rollercoaster day, pushing into positive territory in the middle of the session before finishing 0.4 percent lower. "Something that's going on here that's kind of helping to mitigate the losses is that investors are recalibrating who benefits if Nvidia suffers," said Briefing.com analyst Patrick O'Hare, who pointed to strength in Broadcom and AMD, both of which gained more than five percent. "That's kind of helped soften the blow of Nvidia's problems," O'Hare said. Other tech companies were mixed. AI infrastructure companies Nebius and CoreWeave slumped 16.8 percent and 6.9 percent respectively while tech giants Amazon, Microsoft and Google parent Alphabet all rose. Some analysts said Huang's departure won't affect short-term AI projects already in the works. But FHN Financial's Chris Low noted that the shakeup at Nvidia comes on the heels of US elections earlier this month that showcased public hostility to data centers. "A slowdown in AI development would be a positive thing from an inflation and interest rate perspective," Low said.
